title: Walmart (WMT) Makes Sam's Club Its Exclusive Buy Now Pay Later Checkout Option
detail:
Walmart (WMT) Makes Sam's Club Its Exclusive Buy Now Pay Later Checkout Option
Bailey Pemberton

Walmart (NasdaqGS:WMT) affiliate Sam's Club has signed a multi-year, exclusive buy-now, pay-later partnership with Affirm.

The agreement makes Affirm the sole BNPL provider for Sam's Club members shopping both online and in physical warehouse locations.

The tie-up arrives ahead of the upcoming holiday shopping period, expanding installment payment options for Sam's Club customers.

This exclusive Sam's Club BNPL deal with Affirm is only one piece of the broader Walmart story investors track. Our analysis turns up 2 other big wins for Walmart as well.

For readers looking to explore more ideas around payment and retail infrastructure, this curated set is a useful next step 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

NasdaqGS:WMT Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Oct 2026

Walmart runs a global mix of big-box stores, Sam's Club warehouses, and ecommerce platforms, so agreements like this BNPL partnership fit directly into how its shoppers pay across both physical and digital channels.

How the Affirm deal feeds Walmart's higher margin Narrative

The Walmart Narrative leans on higher margin digital services layered over its huge store base, with payments, memberships and marketplace fees doing more of the heavy lifting. This exclusive BNPL pact with Affirm plugs directly into that idea by giving Sam's Club members another embedded financial service inside the Walmart ecosystem.

"The main factor that has to go right is the continued growth and profitability of higher margin alternative profit pools such as advertising, marketplace services, and membership..."

See how the full story points towards a $127 fair value for Walmart.

This agreement leans into the same thesis that underpins Walmart Connect and Walmart Fulfillment Services. By standardising BNPL through one partner, Walmart can gather cleaner payments data, support e-commerce conversion and potentially tie offers back into Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus without carrying consumer credit risk on its own balance sheet.

The unresolved piece is economics and execution. Management has not detailed how revenue share, bad debt exposure, or regulatory scrutiny around BNPL could affect the profitability of this channel, particularly as Target, Costco and Amazon refine their own checkout stacks. Until those details are clearer, this deal strengthens the alternative profit pool story but leaves the payoff timing and scale open.

For investors, a clear Narrative turns headlines like this BNPL partnership from background noise into a concrete test of whether Walmart is really shifting its business toward richer, fee-based profit streams.

title: Can Walmart's New Bundled Subscription Beat Amazon?
detail:
Can Walmart's New Bundled Subscription Beat Amazon?
Catie Hogan, The Motley Fool

WMT
AMZN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) is offering a bundled subscription deal that could knock Amazon's (NASDAQ: AMZN) Prime membership off its pedestal. Earlier this week, the company announced a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for just $120 per year. That's $100 less than the two programs priced separately, and $19 less than Amazon Prime's $139 cost.

The bundle includes free delivery, 2% Sam's Cash on select purchases, $0.10 off per gallon of gas, and a choice between Peacock and Paramount+ streaming, among other perks. The catch is that it is only available as an annual subscription, and there's no free trial or monthly option available at this time.

Memberships have proven to be lucrative revenue channels for companies like Walmart and Amazon. Shoppers tend to spend significantly more with the merchant when they have a membership, roughly four times as much as non-members in Walmart's case.

So can Walmart's new subscription bundle dethrone Amazon Prime? Probably not. Amazon Prime is so deeply entrenched at this point that the mix of streaming, fast shipping, and ubiquity among consumers is almost immovable. However, Walmart doesn't have to beat Amazon to succeed. This is what investors should focus on.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

This particular offering strengthens Walmart's flywheel and advertising business. Walmart stock trades at a hefty premium, leaving little room for stumbles this holiday season. Some investors may want to wait for a better entry point. Still, overall, Walmart is an incredibly strong business that just created a new product that will help solidify and deepen customer engagement.

Shares of Walmart have risen nearly 6% year to date as of this writing. The stock is trading at roughly 40 times both forward and trailing earnings. The company's e-commerce segment continues to grow substantially, increasing 23% in the fiscal 2027 second quarter. Walmart's membership growth was also impressive at 17%.

Whether it overtakes Amazon or not, Walmart is a worthy investment.

What Happened?

Affirm (AFRM:NASDAQ) signed an exclusive, multi-year deal on October 22 to become Sam's Club's pay-over-time provider, and the stock closed down 1.51% at $72.40 that day. The deal comes about 19 months after Klarna (KLAR) announced it would replace Affirm as Walmart's installment partner.

Since September 23, Affirm has also announced deals with Amazon in the UK, Crate & Barrel, and Ant International's Antom. On October 22, shares closed 15.6% below their highest close of the past year, with fiscal first-quarter results due after the close on November 5.

Affirm Drawdowns (TIKR)
Sam's Club Puts Affirm Back Inside Walmart's Orbit

When Klarna won the Walmart slot in March 2025, Affirm said the integrated Walmart program made up about 5% of its gross merchandise volume (GMV), the value of purchases on its network, and about 2% of adjusted operating income in the six months through December 2024. Walmart (WMT) owns Sam's Club, but terms were not disclosed, so the new deal's size is unknown. Affirm said it will go live on SamsClub.com in the coming weeks and in clubs in 2027, so the September quarter gets nothing from it.

The deal fits two gaps CEO Max Levchin named at a Goldman Sachs conference on September 8. He said Affirm is "still fairly thin in terms of penetration into top 500 e-commerce retailers," then added: "Off-line is still very nascent." Sam's Club offers both, online first and in clubs later. Levchin also said "it's very important for us that no door is better or worse than any other one," so shoppers get basically the same deal across checkout, wallets, and the Affirm Card, with very few exceptions.

On October 22, Levchin told Bloomberg that "every time they pick us, I take it as a vote of confidence." Once Affirm is live, Walmart will work with both rivals across its businesses, which eMarketer noted lets it compare them.

Rate-Hike Fears Moved the Stock More Than the Deal Did

On October 14, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% economists expected. Traders' odds of the Fed holding rates on October 28 fell to 53% from 78.4%, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. The 10-year Treasury yield briefly reached about 5.33% before closing at 5.19%, slightly lower on the day. Affirm fell more than 11.5% at one point, according to Invezz, a steeper drop than other buy now, pay later lenders. Affirm funds loans through warehouse facilities, securitizations, and loan sales, so a higher path for rates raises its cost of capital.

From a September 30 close of $103.92, Walmart is up 16.6% in October with six trading sessions left, which puts it on pace for its best month since 1999. A discount retailer is trading like a growth stock because money is leaving AI and tech, so a buyer at this price is paying as much for the sector rotation as for Walmart's business.

What Getting Back to $1 Trillion Requires

Walmart first passed $1 trillion on February 3, 2026, the first retailer to do so. It hit an intraday record of about $126 a share two weeks after it joined the Nasdaq-100.

With 7.93 billion shares outstanding, a return to breakeven requires roughly $126.05 a share. That is still below the 52-week high of $135.16, so the milestone means recovering lost ground.

Thursday's gain came with no new contract, filing, or guidance change. The most recent reported results are from the second quarter of fiscal 2027, when adjusted EPS of $0.81 beat the $0.7413 consensus.

title: Apple and Alphabet are sending Wall Street different signals
detail:
Apple and Alphabet are sending Wall Street different signals
Hillary Remy, Dana Sullivan Kilroy
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:47 AM PDT 5 min read
AAPL
GOOG
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The two biggest AI bets on Wall Street are not making the same one. One company is writing checks that would strain most national budgets. The other is letting partners do the heavy lifting while it sells the hardware everyone else needs.

Retirement savers feel that split most. A portfolio that is meant to last decades has different needs than a trade meant to pay off next quarter, and the debate comes down to Alphabet versus Apple. Both report earnings this month, so the timing is hard to ignore.

How the Alphabet and Apple gap opened up

Alphabet has lost about $860 billion in market value since its peak, close to Walmart's $937.1 billion, according to 24/7 Wall St., citing an October 17 post by Charlie Bilello of Creative Planning that put Apple at an all-time high and Alphabet 17% below.

Apple is worth $4.95 trillion and Alphabet is worth $4.21 trillion. Apple leads the Magnificent Seven this year at 25.26%, against 6.47% for Alphabet, which has also fallen 4.84% in the past month.

Also read: Apple just made a surprising move with a popular product

Apple's run is real. The stock touched an all-time high of $345.34 in September, weeks after John Ternus became CEO on September 1, and was up 25% for the year with a market value just under $5 trillion, according to TheStreet. The iPhone 18 lineup went on sale September 19 with prices raised by $100, and the $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo ships October 23.

Alphabet went the other way after July's earnings. Revenue beat estimates and Google Cloud grew 82% to $24.8 billion, but the company lifted its 2026 capex outlook to $195 billion to $205 billion, up from $180 billion to $190 billion, and the stock sank.

The next test arrives on October 28. Alphabet brought in $119.8 billion in second-quarter sales, up 24%, yet Bank of America expects about $199 billion of capex this year and $301 billion in 2027, plus a $12.4 billion free cash flow loss in the third quarter. The bank also expects Search growth to cool from 17% to 14% while Cloud accelerates to 93%.

What Alphabet's spending is doing to its cash

Alphabet spent $44.9 billion on capital expenditures in the second quarter, double the year-earlier amount, and posted its first negative free cash flow since going public in 2004, according to Axios, citing FactSet. Net income got a lift from roughly $99 billion in net gains on equity securities.

Alphabet was the first hyperscaler to report this season, Axios noted, so investors read its spending as a signal for the group.

To pay for the buildout, Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion in equity in June, including a $10 billion private placement to Berkshire Hathaway at $351.81 per Class A share and $348.20 per Class C share, Bloomberg reported. The company said demand for its AI services exceeds the supply it can deliver.

If you own Kroger (KR), or are weighing the stock after its 8.2% rise in the five sessions to October 22, 2026, your position most likely sits alongside capital tracking the S&P 500. Every day the index fluctuates, Kroger's performance blends with the rest of those holdings. So does Kroger add to the risk you already carry, or work against it?

Kroger Stock Has Moved Against The Market

Over the past year, from October 21, 2025, to October 22, 2026, Kroger shares moved against the broader market. A $10,000 holding in Kroger fell about $35 on an average day the S&P 500 rose, and gained about $43 on an average day the index declined. For each 1% the S&P 500 moved over the past year, Kroger tended to shift about 0.71% the other way.

That dynamic does not make Kroger a calm stock. Its volatility, the typical size of its swings over a year, was 29.8%, more than double the S&P 500's 12.7%. While Kroger steadied a broader market portfolio over the past year, the shares brought larger swings of their own.

Will Kroger Keep Moving Like This?

Kroger is reshaping its operations during a period of slow sales growth, which gives investors more to weigh. In September 2026, management lowered its full-year forecast for identical sales without fuel, its measure of sales growth at existing stores, to 0.5% at the midpoint from 1.5%. The company maintained its full-year profit forecast.

Kroger laid out a multi-year plan on October 20, 2026, introducing new long-term targets that run through 2029. Management expects its planned acquisition of Giant Eagle to close in 2027. Separately, Albertsons is seeking $8 billion from Kroger over their failed merger, with a trial looming, news reports said on October 12, 2026.

The direction of Kroger's moves is less settled than their size. From October 2021 to October 2026, the stock's daily moves showed almost no connection to the index, posting a correlation of 0.05, where zero means no link. Moving against the broader market is a recent pattern for Kroger, while its wide swings have persisted longer.

Has Kroger Stock Paid You For Its Swings?

Over the five years from October 23, 2021, to October 22, 2026, Kroger paid you slightly more than the market, but yielded less for each unit of swing. The stock returned 13.5% a year during that window, compared with 12.6% for the S&P 500. Kroger posted an annual volatility of 27.4%, against 17.0% for the index.

Dividing the return by the volatility reveals how much each unit of swing earned: 0.493 for Kroger and 0.741 for the S&P 500. A higher figure means the swings paid better, so the market rewarded you more for each unit of swing.
